title: Two 2048-bit RSA Keys, One GCD, Both Broken: Check Your Own Public Keys in the Browser
gist: VIDRAFT's KeyGuard is a browser-only tool that checks RSA public keys for four structural defect families (shared primes via GCD, close primes via Fermat, ROCA fingerprint, weak length/exponent). The piece argues weak RSA keys come from poor entropy at device first boot, mostly in self-signed embedded-device certificates, and reports 65/65 weak keys caught with 0 false alarms on its benchmark.

themes.theme: Weak RSA keys come from bad randomness

insights.claim: 2048-bit RSA keys are safe against today's factoring only if their primes are chosen well; if two devices share a prime a single GCD breaks both, and if primes are too close a 2048-bit key falls in about a millisecond.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Key length is not a proxy for security in embedded fleets; audit key generation quality.
insights.quote: When a device picks them badly, the key length stops mattering.

insights.claim: Routers, cameras and other embedded devices often generate RSA keys right after first boot when little randomness is available, so different devices can land on the same prime.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: IoT/device makers carry latent cryptographic liability from first-boot entropy.
insights.locator: The problem is not RSA. It is how some keys are born

insights.claim: The 2012 USENIX Security study 'Mining Your Ps and Qs' obtained private keys for about 0.50% of TLS hosts because their public keys shared factors.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Shared-factor weakness is measured at internet scale, not theoretical.
insights.locator: Mining Your Ps and Qs, USENIX Security 2012

insights.claim: Keyfactor in 2019 broke 249,553 distinct RSA keys, about 1 in 172 of internet-collected RSA certificates, but found shared factors in only five of about 100 million Certificate Transparency certificates.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Public-CA-issued certs are healthy; risk concentrates in self-signed device certificates.
insights.quote: 249,553 distinct keys broken, about 1 in 172 of the internet-collected RSA certificates

insights.claim: ROCA (CVE-2017-15361) keys from a flawed chip library carry a recognizable mathematical fingerprint detectable via a membership test modulo 38 odd primes.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Legacy hardware with ROCA-affected libraries remains detectable and should be retired.

insights.claim: On a 145-key benchmark (80 healthy, 65 weak), KeyGuard's combined checks found 65/65 weak keys with 0 false alarms in 73 ms, versus 38.5% for size/exponent checks alone and 30.8% each for GCD-only or Fermat-only.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Layered detectors are needed; single-method key audits miss most weak keys.

insights.claim: KeyGuard's ROCA detection flagged 12 of 12 generated ROCA-structured keys with 0 false alarms on 40 ordinary 1024-bit keys.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Validates the ROCA check, though on a small synthetic sample.
insights.locator: We also ran two further checks

insights.claim: A batch-GCD engine processed 220,713 keys (220,707 real Certificate Transparency RSA keys plus 6 planted weak keys) in 122.5 seconds, finding all 6 planted keys with 0 false alarms.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Fleet-scale shared-prime screening is computationally cheap — minutes, not days.

insights.claim: In the demo, a close-prime 2048-bit RSA key was recovered via Fermat factorization in 1.4 ms in a normal browser tab.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Close-prime defects are trivially exploitable on commodity hardware.
insights.locator: See it: a 2048-bit key in about a millisecond

insights.claim: KeyGuard runs all checks in browser JavaScript using native big integers; the authors recorded 0 network requests after page load, with no account or upload.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Client-side security tooling lowers data-handling friction for enterprise audit use.

insights.claim: VIDRAFT positions KeyGuard for device makers checking production batches before shipping, IoT/network operators auditing self-signed certificates, and security teams as a first triage step, since shared primes only appear when keys are compared together.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Pre-ship batch key auditing is an underused QA step for hardware vendors.
insights.quote: A shared prime shows up only when keys are compared with each other.
